title: Kestrel and the Regiment
premise: In the winter of 1813, Gideon Crane, a battlefield nurse who secretly records the names of soldiers erased from official regimental ledgers, is left an infant at his infirmary door with a note instructing him to forget the child's face. The baby belongs to Colonel Ashworth's dead mistress, and powerful men will burn the workshop—and everyone in it—to keep the bloodline quiet. As Gideon shelters the child and falls for Eliza Vane, the colonel's estranged daughter sent to retrieve it, he must choose between finishing his ledger of the forgotten and saving the one life no record can protect. In the end, Gideon trades his ledger to the corrupt adjutant in exchange for safe passage, sends the child away with Eliza under a new name, and remains behind to face a court-martial—only for his stolen pages to surface publicly, toppling the officers who thought silence was theirs to command.
about_author: Freya Eastwick is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing military hospital records from the Peninsular War before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted tollhouse on the Yorkshire moors, where she keeps her own ledger of names found in margins.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Names
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A freezing night in the regimental infirmary introduces Gideon, his hidden notebook of erased soldiers, and the careful silences that keep him alive. He tends a dying private whose name the officers refuse to record. Emotional beat: quiet defiance established—the reader learns what Gideon risks every time ink touches paper.

chapters.title: What the Door Left Behind
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A servant abandons an infant at the infirmary door with a note: forget this face. Gideon recognizes the Ashworth crest on the swaddling cloth. Against every survival instinct, he takes the child in. Emotional beat: fear warring with compassion; the first crack in five years of practiced invisibility.

chapters.title: The Colonel's Daughter
chapters.summary: Eliza's POV. Eliza Vane arrives at the garrison, ostensibly to nurse, actually dispatched by her father Colonel Ashworth to find and quietly dispose of 'a problem.' She does not yet know what the problem is. Emotional beat: dutiful unease—she senses her father's shame but not its shape.

chapters.title: Two Kinds of Silence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Gideon and Eliza circle each other over the infirmary fire, each hiding something, each recognizing the hiding. The baby cries at night; Gideon claims it's a stray cat. Emotional beat: wary attraction built on mutual deception, charged with what neither says.

chapters.title: Adjutant Hale's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Hale's POV (villain). The adjutant calculates the cost of scandal: a dead mistress, a living heir, a nurse who keeps unauthorized records. He begins compiling his own list—of people to remove. Emotional beat: cold menace; power revealed as bookkeeping of lives.

chapters.title: Ashes in the Record Room
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon discovers someone has been burning loose papers from the regimental archive—including pages bearing the mistress's name. He realizes his own ledger could be next, or worse, evidence against him. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into resolve; the stakes become archival and mortal at once.

chapters.title: A Name for the Child
chapters.summary: Gideon and Eliza POV, alternating scenes. Eliza discovers the baby during a night vigil; instead of reporting it, she helps feed it. They christen her privately—Kestrel, after the bird that hovers against the wind. Emotional beat: complicity becomes tenderness; love begins where conspiracy starts.

chapters.title: The Father's Confession
chapters.summary: Eliza's POV. Eliza confronts Colonel Ashworth and learns the truth: the child is his granddaughter by a woman he ruined and abandoned, now conveniently dead. He orders Eliza to bring the baby to him alone. Emotional beat: filial loyalty curdling into horror; duty revealed as a cage.

chapters.title: Hale Makes His Offer
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Adjutant Hale offers Gideon promotion and protection in exchange for the ledger and the child, making explicit what happens to nurses who refuse. Gideon stalls, buying three days. Emotional beat: terror managed through performance; Gideon's gift for silence becomes a weapon.

chapters.title: Three Days
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV rotation. Gideon, Eliza, and the workshop's orderlies plan an escape route through the marsh while maintaining normal routines. Each chapter section ends with someone almost caught. Emotional beat: breathless clock-ticking tension; community forming in secret.

chapters.title: The Informer
chapters.summary: Orderly Thomas's POV. A frightened young orderly, squeezed by debts, betrays the plan to Hale. Guilt-ridden, he confesses to Gideon too late—the escape window is closing. Emotional beat: tragedy of small corruption; the theme of compromised men doing harm cheaply.

chapters.title: Fire at the Workshop
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Hale's men torch the infirmary storehouse as a warning. Gideon saves the ledger from the flames, burning his hands. The workshop's future is now measured in hours. Emotional beat: grief and fury fused; the cost of resistance made visible in ash.

chapters.title: What Eliza Chose
chapters.summary: Eliza's POV. Eliza openly defies her father, renouncing her allowance and name, and asks Gideon—not for escape—but to let her carry Kestrel out herself. Their love is spoken aloud for the first time, with no promise of reunion. Emotional beat: love against duty resolved into action; heartbreak accepted willingly.

chapters.title: The Bargain
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon offers Hale the entire ledger—five years of erased names—in exchange for letting the child and one cart leave unmolested. Hale agrees, planning betrayal. Emotional beat: sacrifice without heroics; Gideon gives up his life's work to save one unrecorded life.

chapters.title: Cart Through the Marsh
chapters.summary: Eliza's POV. The flight through fog and reed-beds, pursued by Hale's riders who were never going to honor the bargain. A near-capture at the ford; a sympathetic dragoon looks the other way. Emotional beat: desperate hope; the natural world indifferent to human schemes.

chapters.title: Court-Martial
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon stands trial for theft of regimental property and falsification of records. He refuses to name the child or Eliza, using the hearing to read selected names aloud into the official transcript—smuggling his ledger into the record itself. Emotional beat: defiant dignity; silence inverted into testimony.

chapters.title: Hale Overreaches
chapters.summary: Hale's POV. Hale, certain of victory, burns the ledger publicly—but the court-martial transcript already circulates among officers' wives and a London correspondent. His patrons begin distancing themselves. Emotional beat: villain undone by his own need to destroy evidence; power eating itself.

chapters.title: The Colonel's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Ashworth's POV. Confronted by the transcript and his own conscience, the colonel publicly acknowledges the child, shattering Hale's legal basis for pursuit—but it costs Ashworth his career and health. Emotional beat: late, insufficient redemption; corruption's bill finally presented.

chapters.title: Sentence
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Struck from the rolls and stripped of rank, Gideon expects prison, but public sympathy and the transcript force a lenient discharge. He walks out of the garrison with nothing but his burned hands and a free mind. Emotional beat: hollow triumph; freedom that feels like exile.

chapters.title: The Road North
chapters.summary: Eliza's POV. In a Yorkshire village, Eliza builds a life under a borrowed name, Kestrel growing and asking questions. A letter arrives with no signature—only a pressed kestrel feather. Emotional beat: tentative peace; waiting transformed into faith.

chapters.title: Names Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. In London, a reformist newspaper prints the full list of forgotten soldiers, crediting 'a nurse of the 44th.' Gideon watches his five years of secret ink become public memory, then turns north without ceremony. Emotional beat: vindication refused as glory; purpose completed quietly.

chapters.title: Kestrel and the Regiment
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, final scene. Gideon reaches the Yorkshire cottage at dusk; Eliza opens the door before he knocks. Kestrel, now talking, asks who he is. He answers: 'Someone who writes things down so they're remembered.' Emotional beat: homecoming earned; identity chosen over identity assigned—the ledger closed, the family opened.
